title: Which are sources of heat?
stem:
Athe Sun
Ba burning candle
Ca switched-on iron
Dan ice cube

Which of the above are sources of heat?
key: A source of heat produces heat: the Sun, burning things, switched-on appliances and rubbing. Ice produces none.

options.text: A, B, C and D
options.pick: Ice seems to give out cold, so it seems to be a source of something.
options.why: Ice produces no heat, and there is no such thing as "cold" flowing out. Ice feels cold because it takes heat from your hand.

options.text: A, B and C only
options.pick: Ask of each one: does it produce heat?
options.why: The Sun, a burning candle and a switched-on iron all produce heat. An ice cube produces none.

options.text: A and B only
options.pick: Only things with a flame or the Sun seem to give heat.
options.why: A switched-on iron is an electrical appliance that produces heat, so it is a source too.

options.text: A only
options.pick: The Sun is the one heat source everyone knows.
options.why: Burning things and switched-on appliances also produce heat.

title: Two beakers at 60 °C
stem:
Beaker A has 100 mL of water at 60 °C. Beaker B has 50 mL of water at 60 °C.

Which statement is correct?
key: Temperature is how hot something is. More water at the same temperature holds more heat.

options.text: They have the same amount of heat, because they have the same temperature.
options.pick: The same reading seems to mean the same heat.
options.why: Temperature does not tell you the amount of heat. More water at the same temperature holds more heat.

options.text: A has a higher temperature, because it has more water.
options.pick: More water seems to mean more hotness.
options.why: The thermometer reads 60 °C in both. The amount of water does not change how hot it is.

options.text: They have the same temperature, but A has more heat.
options.pick: Temperature is how hot; heat is energy. Which one depends on the amount of water?
options.why: Both are equally hot (60 °C), but warming 100 mL to 60 °C took more heat than warming 50 mL.

options.text: B has more heat, because a smaller amount heats up faster.
options.pick: The smaller beaker warms up quicker, which seems to mean more heat.
options.why: It warms quicker because it needs less heat. It holds less heat than A.

title: What is heat?
stem: Which statement about heat is correct?
key: Heat is a form of energy. It is not matter, and "cold" does not flow.

options.text: Heat is a form of energy.
options.pick: Recall what heat is, not how it feels.
options.why: Heat is energy. It can flow from one object to another and change their temperature.

options.text: Heat is the temperature of an object.
options.pick: Heat and temperature both seem to mean how hot something is.
options.why: Temperature measures how hot something is. Heat is the energy that flows.

options.text: Heat is a substance that flows like water.
options.pick: Heat "flows", so it seems to be some kind of stuff.
options.why: Heat is not matter. It has no mass and takes up no space.

options.text: Cold is a form of energy that flows into warm objects.
options.pick: Cold things seem to give out coldness.
options.why: Only heat flows. Cold is simply less heat.

title: A cup of hot tea
stem:
A cup of hot tea is left on a table in a room at 30 °C.

What happens to the tea?
key: Heat flows from hotter to colder until both are at the same temperature.

options.text: It loses heat until it is colder than the room.
options.pick: Once it starts cooling, it seems to keep cooling.
options.why: Heat stops flowing when the tea reaches the room's temperature. It cannot cool below it this way.

options.text: Cold from the room flows into the tea.
options.pick: The room is cooler, so its coolness seems to move in.
options.why: Nothing called "cold" flows. Heat flows out of the tea.

options.text: It stays hot, because heat stays inside liquids.
options.pick: Hot drinks often stay warm for a while.
options.why: Heat keeps flowing out until the tea and the room are at the same temperature.

options.text: It loses heat to the surroundings until it reaches 30 °C.
options.pick: Heat flows from hotter to colder. When does it stop?
options.why: Heat flows from the hot tea to the cooler room until both are at the same temperature.

title: Ice in juice
stem:
Ice cubes are put into a glass of juice, and the juice becomes colder.

Why?
key: The juice gets colder because it loses heat to the colder ice.

options.text: The ice gives coldness to the juice.
options.pick: Ice seems to spread its cold.
options.why: There is no "coldness" to give. The juice gets colder by losing heat.

options.text: The juice loses heat to the ice.
options.pick: Which is hotter, the juice or the ice? Which way does heat flow?
options.why: Heat flows from the warmer juice to the colder ice. The juice loses heat, so its temperature falls.

options.text: The juice gains heat from the ice.
options.pick: The ice and juice are swapping something, and heat is the word used.
options.why: Gaining heat would make the juice warmer. It got colder, so it lost heat.

options.text: Both the ice and the juice gain heat.
options.pick: The ice melts, so heat seems to be involved everywhere.
options.why: The ice gains heat, but the juice loses it. That is why the juice's temperature falls.

key: A falling temperature means the object is losing heat.

options.text: It gained coldness from the room.
options.pick: The room is cooler, so it seems to give coolness.
options.why: Cold does not flow. The water lost heat.

options.text: It gained heat, because its temperature changed.
options.pick: Something changed, and heat seems to be the cause of all change.
options.why: A temperature that falls means heat was lost, not gained.

options.text: It lost heat, so its temperature fell.
options.pick: The line goes down. Is the water gaining or losing heat?
options.why: A falling temperature means the water was losing heat to the cooler room.

options.text: Its heat stayed the same; only its temperature changed.
options.pick: Heat and temperature seem to be separate, so one could change alone.
options.why: The temperature fell because heat left the water. The two go together.

title: The ball and the ring
stem:
A metal ball just passes through a metal ring. After the ball is heated, it cannot pass through.

Which statement is correct?
key: Gaining heat makes things expand. Their volume changes; their mass stays the same.

options.text: The ball expanded and became heavier.
options.pick: Bigger seems to mean heavier.
options.why: Expansion increases volume, not mass.

options.text: The ring contracted, because the ball became hot.
options.pick: Something must have got smaller to stop the ball.
options.why: The ring was not heated. The ball expanded because it gained heat.

options.text: The ball contracted when it gained heat.
options.pick: Heating seems to tighten things.
options.why: Gaining heat makes things expand, not contract.

options.text: The ball expanded when it gained heat, and its mass stayed the same.
options.pick: Gaining heat makes things expand. Does expanding change the mass?
options.why: The ball's volume increased, so it no longer fits. Its mass did not change.

title: A melting ice block
stem:
A block of ice on a plate slowly melts in a room.

Which statement is correct?
key: Melting needs heat gain. The ice gains heat from the warmer room.

options.text: The ice gains heat from the surroundings and melts.
options.pick: Melting is a change of state. Does it need heat gain or heat loss?
options.why: The warmer room gives heat to the ice. Gaining heat makes it melt.

options.text: The ice loses heat and melts.
options.pick: The ice seems to "give up" something as it disappears.
options.why: Melting needs heat gain. Losing heat would keep it frozen.

options.text: The ice loses its coldness to the air.
options.pick: The ice seems to give its cold away.
options.why: There is no coldness to lose. The ice gains heat.

options.text: The surroundings gain heat from the ice.
options.pick: Heat seems to come out of the ice as it changes.
options.why: The ice is colder than the room, so heat flows into the ice, not out of it.

title: The metal and wooden spoons
stem:
A metal spoon and a wooden spoon have been in the same room for a long time. The metal spoon feels colder to touch.

Why?
key: Both spoons are at room temperature. Metal is a good conductor, so it takes heat from your hand faster.

options.text: The metal spoon is at a lower temperature.
options.pick: It feels colder, so it seems to be colder.
options.why: Both have reached room temperature. The difference is how fast heat leaves your hand.

options.text: Wood is a good conductor of heat, so it feels warmer.
options.pick: The wood feels warm, so it seems to pass heat well.
options.why: Wood is a poor conductor. It takes heat from your hand slowly, so it does not feel cold.

options.text: Metal is a good conductor of heat, so it conducts heat away from the hand faster.
options.pick: Both have been in the room for ages. Are their temperatures really different?
options.why: Both are at room temperature. The metal takes heat from your hand faster, so it feels colder.

options.text: The metal gives out coldness.
options.pick: Cold metal seems to spread cold to your hand.
options.why: Nothing gives out cold. The metal takes heat from your hand.

options.pick: 35 is the nearest number to the top of the liquid.
options.why: The liquid is above the 35 mark. Count the small marks above it.

options.pick: Each short mark is 1 °C. Count up from 35.
options.why: The liquid stops two short marks above 35, at 37 °C.

options.pick: Counted the marks, but started the count at the 35 mark itself.
options.why: The 35 mark is zero extra. Two marks above it is 37.

options.pick: Read from the 45 mark instead of the 35 mark.
options.why: Check which labelled number is just below the liquid: it is 35, not 45.

title: Which is a source of heat?
stem: Which of these is a source of heat?
key: A source of heat produces heat. Ice, the Moon and switched-off appliances produce none.

options.text: A bag of ice
options.pick: Ice seems to give out cold.
options.why: Ice produces no heat, and cold is not something that is given out.

options.text: A switched-off toaster
options.pick: A toaster is a heating appliance.
options.why: It produces heat only while it is switched on.

options.text: A switched-on hairdryer
options.pick: Which one produces heat right now?
options.why: A switched-on electrical appliance produces heat.

options.text: The Moon
options.pick: The Moon shines like the Sun.
options.why: The Moon only reflects sunlight. It produces no heat of its own.

title: Rubbing your hands
stem:
Rubbing your hands together makes them warm.

What is the source of heat?
key: Rubbing two things together produces heat.

options.text: The rubbing between the hands
options.pick: What is happening that was not happening before?
options.why: Rubbing two things together produces heat.

options.text: The air around the hands
options.pick: The air touches the hands.
options.why: The air is not producing heat. The rubbing is.

options.text: There is no source; the hands were already warm.
options.pick: Hands are always warm.
options.why: The hands get warmer while you rub, so the rubbing is producing heat.

options.text: The cold leaves the hands.
options.pick: Warming up seems to mean the cold goes away.
options.why: Cold does not move. The hands gain heat produced by the rubbing.

title: A bathtub and a cup
stem:
A bathtub of water and a cup of water are both at 40 °C.

Which statement is correct?
key: Same temperature, more water: more heat.

options.text: They have the same amount of heat.
options.pick: The same temperature seems to mean the same heat.
options.why: More water at the same temperature holds more heat.

options.text: The cup has a higher temperature, because it is smaller.
options.pick: Small things seem to heat up more.
options.why: Both thermometers read 40 °C. Size does not change the reading.

options.text: The bathtub has a higher temperature, because it has more water.
options.pick: More water seems to mean hotter.
options.why: Both are at 40 °C. The bathtub has more heat, not a higher temperature.

options.text: They have the same temperature, but the bathtub has more heat.
options.pick: Which depends on the amount of water: temperature or heat?
options.why: Both are equally hot, but the bathtub's much larger amount of water holds far more heat.

title: Same water, different temperatures
stem:
Beakers A and B each hold 200 mL of water. A is at 30 °C and B is at 70 °C.

Which has more heat?
key: Same amount of water, higher temperature: more heat.

options.text: A
options.pick: A is cooler, so it seems to hold heat better.
options.why: A is cooler, so it has less heat.

options.text: B
options.pick: The amounts are the same. Which one is hotter?
options.why: With the same amount of water, the hotter one holds more heat.

options.text: They have the same heat, because they hold the same amount of water.
options.pick: The same amount seems to mean the same heat.
options.why: The temperature matters too. B is hotter, so it has more heat.

options.text: It cannot be known without measuring their heat on a balance.
options.pick: Amounts are usually measured on a balance.
options.why: A balance measures mass. Same amount and higher temperature means more heat.

title: A hot block in water
stem:
A metal block at 90 °C is put into water at 30 °C in a closed, well-insulated container.

What happens?
key: Heat flows from hotter to colder until both reach the same temperature, somewhere in between.

options.text: Heat flows from the block to the water until both reach the same temperature, between 30 °C and 90 °C.
options.pick: Heat flows from hotter to colder. When does it stop, and where?
options.why: The block cools and the water warms until they are equal. They meet somewhere in between.

options.text: They swap: the block ends at 30 °C and the water at 90 °C.
options.pick: The heat seems to move completely from one to the other.
options.why: Heat stops flowing as soon as the temperatures are equal. They meet in between.

options.text: Both end at 90 °C.
options.pick: The hot block seems to heat everything to its own temperature.
options.why: The block loses heat as the water gains it, so the block's temperature falls.

options.text: Cold flows from the water into the block.
options.pick: The water is colder, so it seems to cool the block by sending cold.
options.why: Only heat flows, from the block into the water.

title: A cold drink on the table
stem:
A cold drink at 5 °C is left on a table in a room at 30 °C.

Hours later, what is its temperature most likely to be?
key: The drink gains heat from the room until it reaches the room's temperature.

options.text: Lower than 5 °C, because it gives its cold to the room
options.pick: The drink seems to spread its cold out.
options.why: The drink gains heat. It does not give out cold.

options.text: 5 °C, because it stays cold
options.pick: Cold drinks seem to stay cold.
options.why: Heat keeps flowing in from the warmer room until the temperatures are equal.

options.pick: Heat flows into the drink until when?
options.why: The drink gains heat from the room until it reaches the room's temperature.

options.text: Higher than 30 °C
options.pick: It keeps warming up, so it seems it could go past the room temperature.
options.why: Heat stops flowing once the drink reaches 30 °C. It cannot go higher this way.

title: Datalogger readings
stem:
A temperature sensor and datalogger recorded the temperature of some water in a beaker.

What happened to the water?
key: A rising temperature means the water gained heat.

options.text: It lost heat.
options.pick: Heat seems to be used up as time passes.
options.why: Losing heat would make the temperature fall. It rose.

options.text: It lost coldness.
options.pick: Getting warmer seems to mean losing cold.
options.why: There is no coldness. The water gained heat.

options.text: Only its temperature changed, not its heat.
options.pick: Heat and temperature are different things.
options.why: They are different, but a temperature rise is caused by gaining heat.

options.text: It gained heat.
options.pick: The temperature went up.
options.why: A rising temperature means the water gained heat.

title: Heated water's mass
stem:
A bottle of water is warmed and the water expands.

What happens to the mass of the water?
key: Expanding changes the volume, not the mass. Heat has no mass.

options.text: It increases, because the volume increased.
options.pick: Bigger seems to mean heavier.
options.why: The water takes up more space but has the same mass.

options.text: It stays the same.
options.pick: Expanding changes the volume. Does anything get added?
options.why: No water is added or lost, so the mass stays the same.

options.text: It decreases, because the water spreads out.
options.pick: Spread-out things seem lighter.
options.why: Spreading out changes the volume only. The mass stays the same.

options.text: It increases, because the water gained heat, and heat has mass.
options.pick: Something was added, so the mass seems to go up.
options.why: Heat is energy, not matter. It has no mass.

title: Railway tracks
stem: Why are small gaps left between sections of a railway track?
key: Tracks expand on hot days. The gaps give them room.

options.text: So the tracks can expand on hot days without bending
options.pick: When do metal tracks get bigger?
options.why: The tracks gain heat on hot days and expand. The gaps give them room.

options.text: So the tracks can contract on hot days
options.pick: The tracks change size in the heat.
options.why: Gaining heat makes them expand, not contract.

options.text: So the tracks become lighter when they expand
options.pick: Gaps seem to save weight.
options.why: Expansion does not change mass. The gaps are space to expand into.

options.text: So the tracks have room to expand on cold nights
options.pick: Temperature changes at night too.
options.why: On cold nights the tracks lose heat and contract. They expand on hot days.

title: Bottles not filled to the top
stem: Why are bottled drinks never filled right to the top?
key: Liquids expand when they gain heat. The space stops the container from bursting.

options.text: To leave room for the drink to contract on hot days
options.pick: Liquids change size in the heat.
options.why: Gaining heat makes the drink expand, not contract.

options.text: So the drink weighs less when it is hot
options.pick: A hot drink seems lighter.
options.why: The mass does not change when the drink expands.

options.text: To leave room for the drink to expand when it gains heat
options.pick: What happens to a liquid when it gets warmer?
options.why: The drink expands when it gains heat. The space stops the bottle from bursting.

options.text: Because liquids expand when they are cooled
options.pick: Cooling seems to make a liquid swell.
options.why: A cooled liquid loses heat and contracts.

title: A cloth drying in the sun
stem:
A wet cloth hung in the sun becomes dry.

What happens to the water?
key: Evaporation needs heat gain.

options.text: It loses heat and changes into water vapour.
options.pick: The water seems to give something up as it disappears.
options.why: Evaporation needs heat gain, not heat loss.

options.text: It gains heat and changes into water vapour.
options.pick: Liquid water changes to a gas. Does that need heat gain or heat loss?
options.why: The water gains heat from the Sun and the air, and evaporates into water vapour.

options.text: It loses heat and soaks deeper into the cloth.
options.pick: The water seems to hide inside the cloth.
options.why: The water leaves the cloth as water vapour, after gaining heat.

options.text: It gains coldness from the air.
options.pick: Drying can feel cool.
options.why: There is no coldness. The water gains heat and evaporates.

title: Drops on a cold glass
stem:
Water droplets form on the outside of a glass of iced water.

What happens to the water vapour in the air?
key: Water vapour condenses when it loses heat.

options.text: It gains heat from the glass and changes into water.
options.pick: Something changes state, so heat seems to be gained.
options.why: The glass is colder, so the water vapour loses heat to it.

options.text: It gains coldness from the glass and changes into water.
options.pick: The cold glass seems to pass its cold on.
options.why: Nothing cold flows. The water vapour loses heat.

options.text: It loses heat and changes into ice.
options.pick: Losing heat seems to mean freezing.
options.why: It loses enough heat to condense into liquid water, not to freeze.

options.text: It loses heat to the cold glass and changes into water.
options.pick: The gas becomes liquid. Does that need heat gain or heat loss?
options.why: The water vapour touches the cold glass, loses heat and condenses into droplets.

title: A frying pan handle
stem: Which material is most suitable for the handle of a frying pan?
key: A handle needs a poor conductor of heat, such as plastic or wood.

options.text: Plastic
options.pick: The handle must stop heat from reaching your hand.
options.why: Plastic is a poor conductor, so little heat flows along the handle to your hand.

options.text: Steel, because it is a good conductor of heat
options.pick: Good conductor sounds like a good thing.
options.why: A good conductor would carry heat straight to your hand. The handle needs a poor conductor.

options.text: Copper, because metals are good for cooking
options.pick: The pan is metal, so the handle seems fine as metal.
options.why: The pan is metal so heat reaches the food. The handle needs the opposite.

options.text: Aluminium, because it is light
options.pick: A light handle is easy to hold.
options.why: Aluminium is a metal and a good conductor, so the handle would get hot.

title: A metal cooking pot
stem: Why are cooking pots made of metal?
key: Metal is a good conductor, so heat flows quickly through the pot to the food.

options.text: Metal is a good conductor of heat, so heat flows quickly to the food.
options.pick: What does a pot need to do with the heat from the stove?
options.why: Heat flows easily through metal from the flame to the food.

options.text: Metal is a poor conductor, so it keeps the heat in.
options.pick: Keeping heat in sounds useful for cooking.
options.why: Metal is a good conductor. Heat flows through it easily.

options.text: Metal produces heat of its own.
options.pick: Metal pots get very hot.
options.why: The pot gets hot because heat flows into it from the stove. It is not a source.

options.text: Metal stops cold from getting into the food.
options.pick: Pots protect the food.
options.why: Cold does not flow. The pot lets heat flow into the food.

options.why: The liquid is two marks above 20: 20 + 2 + 2 = 24 °C.

options.why: Count the spaces above 20, not the marks including 20.

title: Measuring how hot
stem: Which should you use to find out how hot a beaker of water is?
key: A thermometer measures temperature. Touch is not reliable.

options.text: A measuring cylinder
options.pick: It is the usual apparatus for water.
options.why: A measuring cylinder measures volume, not temperature.

options.text: An electronic balance
options.pick: Balances give a reading for anything.
options.why: A balance measures mass, not temperature.

options.text: Your hand
options.pick: You can feel whether water is hot.
options.why: Touch is not reliable. It only tells you how fast heat moves to or from your hand.

options.text: A thermometer
options.pick: How hot something is is its temperature.
options.why: A thermometer measures temperature in °C.

title: A thermometer moved into cold water
stem:
A thermometer is moved from warm water into cold water, and its reading falls.

Why?
key: Losing heat makes the liquid in a thermometer contract, so the reading falls.

options.text: The liquid gains heat and contracts.
options.pick: Something changed, so heat seems to be gained.
options.why: The water is colder, so the liquid loses heat.

options.text: The liquid gains coldness from the water.
options.pick: Cold water seems to make things cold by passing cold on.
options.why: Nothing cold flows. The liquid loses heat.

options.text: The liquid in the thermometer loses heat and contracts.
options.pick: The reading falls. What happens to a liquid that loses heat?
options.why: In the cold water, the liquid in the thermometer loses heat, contracts, and moves down the tube.

options.text: The liquid loses heat and expands.
options.pick: Losing heat changes the liquid's size.
options.why: Losing heat makes it contract, which is why the level falls.
